strengths: Introduces a substantial, well-controlled behavioral dataset (72 subjects, 1020 trials, eye-tracking enforced fixation) that meaningfully scales up a classical two-dot psychophysics paradigm to naturalistic COCO images, providing a valuable resource for the community.

Careful experimental design, including matched same/different distances to rule out simple distance confounds, manual verification of object boundaries, and eye-tracking-based fixation control, lends strong credibility to the behavioral data.

The proposed ROC-based object-centricity metric is simple, interpretable, and requires no additional supervision, making it broadly applicable for probing patch-level representations in any vision model.

The comparison across a well-chosen diverse set of models (DINO family, MAE, supervised ViT/ConvNeXt, distilled ConvNeXt) isolates the effect of training objective versus architecture in a clean, controlled manner, yielding a clear and consistent finding (objective > architecture).

The Gram-alignment distillation experiment is a nice causal/interventional complement to the correlational analyses, and its convergence with DINOv3's own reported motivation for Gram anchoring strengthens the paper's mechanistic claims.
The paper is clearly written, well organized, and the figures (affinity maps, ROC curves, behavioral condition breakdowns) effectively support the narrative.
weaknesses: Only ViT-Base and ConvNeXt-Base are tested; there is no exploration of model scale (e.g., ViT-L/g or larger DINOv3 variants) which could confound 'objective' effects with capacity, and would strengthen claims about generality.

The readout used to predict same/different judgments and RTs is a simple 2-layer MLP trained on ~30k COCO-derived synthetic trials; details of this readout (architecture, training details, hyperparameter selection, sensitivity to design choices) are sparse, limiting reproducibility and interpretability of the reported grouping accuracies and correlations.

The Gram-alignment distillation procedure (loss formulation, training schedule, hyperparameters, and whether ImageNet classification accuracy is preserved) is not described in sufficient detail in the main text, making the central mechanistic claim harder to fully verify or reproduce.

Statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals or significance tests comparing models' normalized Spearman correlations, or the object-centricity vs. behavioral-alignment correlation in Fig. 6B) is not reported, so the strength of some comparisons (e.g., DINOv3 vs DINOv2 ViT-B) is unclear.

The behavioral paradigm, while scaled up relative to prior work, still only samples two dot locations per image (center + one peripheral point) and does not capture the full richness of object segmentation (e.g., full-scene segmentation, multi-part object structure), which somewhat limits how strongly the object-centricity metric's real segmentation validity can be assessed against exhaustive human judgments.

The paper would benefit from more direct comparison to other alignment approaches or brain-based benchmarks (e.g., referenced fMRI encoding results) to contextualize how large the reported behavioral alignment gap to the noise ceiling actually is in absolute terms.
